decisive. The Mexican loss was three men
killed and ten horses. The Indians
lost four warriors and six horses.

tackled the Indians in the Pine mountains,
about fifty miles from the New Mexico line.
After a long fight the Indians retired. Their
loss is unknown. The Mexicans lost six
killed. Colonel Wales intends to follow and
attack them again. Heis of the opinion that
they will try and get back to New Mexico, in
which case Colonel Grierson and eight COM
panies of the Tenth cavalry, who are stationed
within forty miles OF their crossing place,
will doubtless be on their trail within few
hours after they cross. 1.

DEATH OF A NOBLE ENGIIsHWoMAN.


Lady Susan Talbot, sister OF the former Earl OF
Shrewsbury and aunt of the last Catholic lord,
died recently in the Dubois private hospital.
Though Of most ancient English nobility, and an
aristocrat in all her tissues, she was woman of
homely manners, and masculine in appearance and
conversation. Her stature was gigantic, and her
build heavy. She walked like q cavalry soldier,
and her chin was hirsute The Prussians taking
her for a man disguised, threw her into jail as
spy and released her only after medical examina-
tion. She had strong temper, a hearty laugh, a
warm heart, and fine, prompt judgment. A
Protestant member of great Catholic family, she
passed most of her life in France; but though
voluntarily estraneed from her relatives, there was
a moment when she wrote to the Lord Chancellor
claiming to be the guardian of the youthful Earl
of Shrewsbury. Her passion was love for dogs and
horses, three of which she groomed herself. Not
withstanding her masculinity. Lady Susan had
sweet blue eyes, and lovely auburn hair, which she
arranged in falling curs.

Death from Coal Gas.-Frederick Teggest
young butcher, living on Garrison lane, near the
Frederick road, 1st district, died on Tuesday after
noon under peculiar circumstances. About 8
o'clock Monday morning, shortly after his
mothers departure for Hanover market, the young
man fastened the door of his room leading into the
hall, and lying down went to sleep, having pre-
viously told his mother to wake him on her return
from market. Mrs. Teggest afterward remembered
that she had closed the damper efthe stove before
she left and that the gas was thus prevented from
escaping up the chimney. When she returned
from market Mt l o'clock in the day the mother
went to her sons room to wake him. She found
the door secured but after rapping on it for several
minutes and receiving no answer, she alarmed the
house. Several members of the family arriving
on the scene broke in the door and were imme-
diately assaulted by the fumes of gas. The room
was filled with it and on the bed young Teggest
was found lying insensible He was taken into
an adjoining room and restoratives applied, but
he still remained unconscious and died Tuesday
afternoon. In the room a canary bird was found
dead, having been poisoned by the noxious gases.
Teggest was single and was well known in the
county, being temperate and kind to his mother,
who is widow.

crop. Cape river rose 20 feet, and its fertile

general prospect for all crops are better

The great pigeon nesting of Forest
county, Pa, covers twenty miles. II is
in jerks and Howe townships, near the
source Of streams that empty into the
Allegheny river. Il is sixteen miles
south of Sheffield, twenty miles west of
Kane, and hundred miles south Of Buff
falo in 4 direct line. The country is
almost an unbroken wilderness. Not
more than ten persons live within the
boundaries Of the. nesting. There are
roads, but they are as rough as Tammany
politicians and surpass them in bruising
power. They were made by wood-chop-
pers and bark -peciers. Roots and stones
mount skyward, and ruts and mud holes
sink deep toward the bottomless pit
The country is neither rocky nor noun
famous. II is a hilly slope, shaded with
beeches and hemlocks, and few cherry,
birch, and maple trees. The beeches
bear crop Of nuts irregularly and new
CT two years in succession. The nut is
triple-sided and triangular, and grows
within prickly burr. much smaller than
4 chestnut burr. Each burr contains
two nuts. The first frost cracks the
burrs, and the nuts drop to the ground
Under covering Of snow they retain
their sweetness until spring.


These nuts attract the pigeons. The
condition Of the crop is studied by small
scouting parties in the fall, and in some
manner is told to the main army, who
advance with the approach Of spring
This year the advance guard appeared
in the latter part OF February. They
roasted At the head OF Minister and
porky creeks, tributaries Of the Tionesta.
4 light snow fell soon after their arrival,
but did not prevent them from securing
IN ample supply Of nuts. They swept
downward in groups of thousands and
whipped the snow from the ground with
their wings. The continuous tapping
sounded like the roar OF 4 cataract.


THE BIRDS RoOsTiNG.


Myriads Of birds poured into the roost
daily for the next fortnight. Theycame
in sheets that stretched from horizon to
horizon, and n, times obscured the light
Of the sun. At night over five square
miles Of trees were loaded with roosting
birds. The noise was deafening. At
times huge branches, broken by the
weight Of birds, crashed to the ground,
throwing the vast camp into dire confu-
sion. The unfortunate pigeons fluttered
to and froin the darkness. uttering plain
tive cries, which w:re answered by their
more fortunate companions in the trees.
a heavy fall Of snow or 4 gale after dark
breaks many overwcightcd limbs and
spreads dismay among the flock. The
fallen birds skulk to cover and await the
break Of day, filling the darkness with
their cries OF terror. Farmers and others
visited the roost after night-fall, and, by
the light Of blazing fire, dubbed hun
dreds Of birds from the lower branches
Of the trees with long poles.


While sojourning at the roost the birds
mate. The tom pigeon COOS incessant-
ly, swelling his chest Ia Conkling and
ruffiing the feathers At his neck. The
mating lasts three or urdays. Athous-
and millions Of birds or more arc court
ing. The forest resounds with love-
making. Frequently toms court the
same hen, and battle royal ensues.-
Eyes fash fire, beaks are crossed like
raplers, and the combatants use their
wings as Irishmen use shillelahs At 1
country fair. The hens stand By, coy
and modest, and give themselves to the
victor without reserve. Once mated,
the pair is a model Of constancy. The
tom is all attention and the hen all al
fection. He brings her the choicest
deliczeies and she rewards him with
kisses. Woe betide the feaihered rouc
who tries to loosen the domestic bond.
Respectable married pigeons make COM
mon cause against him, and club him
from the camp in disgrace The pair,
however, are not mated forlife. A nest
ing breaks the contract, and ever after
ward they treat each other like strangers.
No tom was ever known TO fight twicc
for the same hen. II a hen loses her
mate she remains widow until the next
year.


THE WAY THEY NEST.


Nesting begins soon after mating
The birds never nest at 4 roost. This
year the first corps nested fortnight
after their arrival. The nests are most
ly made in leaaess hard wood trees,
about twenty miles from the roost. The
tom gathers the twigs and the hen in
TERRACES them. No artistic skill is DIS
played. The twigs are woven without
regularity, and the structure resembles
an eagles nest on 4 small scale. The

Mr.. R. t. Joyce, who has the contract fol
carrying the mail from this place to Cleburne


brought the news Tuesday evening that the


United States mail between Cleburne and
Mansfield had been captured and robbed
by three bandits The carrier was pro-

when about half way between those two
places three men, well mounted, rode out into
the road, and throwing their six-shooters
down on him, brought him to q halt. One
of the gang guarded him with his pistol
drawn, while the other two ripped open the
sack and went through the letters and pack
ages, which they threw on the ground when
they were through with them. How much
money they got is not known, though 1t Is
surmised that it was but small amount.
They were all masked, and appeared to
avoid talking as much as possible, speaking
only when 1t was necessary. When they had
gone through the mail they mounted
and rode off in the direction Of Cleburne.
Two of them were riding dark bays and the
other light bay horse. The man on the
light bay had rent in his coat on the left
shoulder. Mr. Joyce thinks he saw the same
parties coming into Dallas Tuesday night.
They rode in front Of him until they struck
the pike leading to the bridge, when they
turned off into the brush. They afterwards
came into the city, and the one with the rent
in his coat tried to sell his horse, but failed.
This is the second robbery that has occurred
within the last two weeks.

limbs, tearing them in a fearful manner

monkey escaped to Wabash avenue, pursued
by crowd, and there hid under the sidewalk.
Martin was rem we'd to doctors office, and

blood, but may survive.

For more than twenty years the cx-
traordinary case Of Susan::S. Godsey,
better known as the "Sleeping Beauty"
has puzzled the most eminent physicians
Of this country and Europe. She was
born in Obion county, Tenn, just across
the State line, and about six miles from
Hickman, Kentucky. Her parents were
extremely poor and living in 4 small
log-house containing only one room.-
Until eight years of age the girl was
strong enough and healthy, and seemed
in nowise remarkable. At that age,
however, she was stricken with fever,
but was attended by an experienced
physician, who soon checked the disease.
The girl sunk into a slumber which last
cd an unusually long time, and finally
awokc weak, but well. To the surprise
Of the family and physician she remain
cd awake but few minutes, when she
again went TO sleep. From that time
forward, 4 period of more than twenty
one years, she has never been awake
more than three minutes NJ time. The
leihargic state invariably lasts 4 certain
number Of hours. She awakcs At six
O'Clock in the morning and at three
O'Clock and eight O'Clock each night,
never varying a one half minute from
the regular time She takes but very
little nourishmcnt. and that only twice
in tweniy-four hours. During the time
in which She sleeps she does not appear
TO breathe, and mirror held against her
nostriS remains untarnished Her
breathing. if indeed she breaihcs at all,
is not sufficient to stir the slightest down
suspended against her nosirils by silken
thread. When her remarkable cond-
tion became known, physicians 1ockcd
from all parts of the country to see her.
None were able satisfactorily, to account
for the phenomenon, although many
theories were advanced. The true cause
has never to this day been determined,
although the woman may still be alter
nately sleeping and waking with the
regularity of clock work. One physi-
clan who visited her continually for six
teen years, frankly confessed that he
could form no opinion regarding the
cause.


She is described aS rather under me-
dium size, and with the exception that
she is sometimes troubled when awake
with neuralgia pains in her head and
neck, and that one arm is slightly par
alyzcd. enjoys as far as she can enjoy
anything, good health. One remarkable
feature of the case is, that while her
hair has grown to great length her finger
nails have not grown any since she was
first stricken. Far from anything re-
pugnant in her appearance, even while
animation is suspended, she would be
considered very pretty lady by those
unacquainted with her condition. She
retains what knowledge she possessed at
eight years Of age, but has not been
awake enough since then to learn any
thing more. She knows her relatives
and friends, and converses with them in
her conscious moments. Before falling
asleep slight hiccough or choking
sound proceeds apparently from her
throat. She then so quickly becomes
inScnSible that she is sometimes unable
10 finish 4 sentence oreven word while
talking \ short time since commit
tee of five physicians were appointed to
watch the subject, and found the case
was just Is it had been represented to be.
